title: The First Missing Quotient
statement: For a positive integer $N$, let $g(N)$ be the least positive integer $k$ such that the equation $\left\lfloor \frac{N}{n} \right\rfloor = k$ has no solution in positive integers $n$. Here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. Find the number of positive integers $N$ for which $g(N) = 20$.
hints: Compare the two neighbouring quotients $\lfloor N/k \rfloor$ and $\lfloor N/(k+1) \rfloor$. What does it say about the value $k$ if they are equal? List the $N$ for which this happens when $k = 20$.

Use floor-function intervals. The value $k$ is missed exactly when $(k+1)q \le N \le kq + k - 1$ for some integer $q \ge 0$. For $k = 20$ this gives blocks of $N$ with $q \le 19$, but $N$ must also avoid the corresponding blocks for every $k \le 19$.

Write $[(k+1)q,\ kq+k-1]$ for the block of $N$ that miss $k$ with common quotient $q$. The blocks for $(k,q) = (19,q), (18,q+1), (17,q+2), (16,q+3)$ join end to end and cover every integer from $20q$ to $16q+63$, which rules out the $k=20$ blocks with $q \le 11$. For $q = 12$, the blocks $(17,14)$ and $(16,15)$ remove $252$ to $255$. For $N \ge 256$, a nonempty block forces $N \le k^2 - 1$, so only $k = 17, 18, 19$ can be missed. It remains to compare those blocks with the $k=20$ blocks and count what survives.
solution: Solution. First we describe when a value is missed. Let $k$ be a positive integer. We have $\lfloor N/n \rfloor = k$ exactly when $\frac{N}{k+1} < n \le \frac{N}{k}$, and any such $n$ is automatically positive. An integer $n$ lies in this range exactly when $\lfloor N/k \rfloor > \lfloor N/(k+1) \rfloor$. Since always $\lfloor N/k \rfloor \ge \lfloor N/(k+1) \rfloor$, the value $k$ is missed exactly when these two floors are equal, say to $q \ge 0$. This is equivalent to $(k+1)q \le N$ and $N < k(q+1)$. Hence $k$ is missed exactly when $N$ lies in the block $$B(k,q) = [(k+1)q,\ kq+k-1]$$ for some integer $q \ge 0$. If $B(k,q)$ is nonempty then $q \le k-1$, so every $N$ in it satisfies $N \le k(k-1)+k-1 = k^2-1$. Now $g(N) = 20$ exactly when $N$ lies in some $B(20,q)$ with $0 \le q \le 19$ and in no block $B(k,q')$ with $k \le 19$. The blocks $B(20,q)$ are $[21q,\ 20q+19]$. Suppose first that $0 \le q \le 11$. The four blocks $$B(19,q) = [20q,\ 19q+18], \quad B(18,q+1) = [19q+19,\ 18q+35],$$ $$B(17,q+2) = [18q+36,\ 17q+50], \quad B(16,q+3) = [17q+51,\ 16q+63]$$ follow one another without gaps, so together they contain every integer from $20q$ to $16q+63$. Since $q \le 11$ gives $20q+19 \le 16q+63$, we have $20q \le 21q \le N \le 20q+19 \le 16q+63$. So $N$ misses one of $16, 17, 18, 19$, and $g(N) \ne 20$. Suppose next that $q = 12$, so $N$ lies in $[252, 259]$. Here $B(17,14) = [252, 254]$ and $B(16,15) = [255, 255]$, so $252$ to $255$ all fail. This leaves $256$ to $259$. All remaining candidates satisfy $N \ge 256$. They are $256$ to $259$, together with the blocks for $q = 13, \dots, 19$: $$[273,279],\ [294,299],\ [315,319],\ [336,339],\ [357,359],\ [378,379],\ [399,399].$$ For such $N$, a missed $k \le 19$ needs $k^2 - 1 \ge 256$, so $k \ge 17$. It therefore suffices to list the blocks for $k = 17, 18, 19$ that reach $256$ or beyond, using $q' \le k-1$. For $k = 17$ they are $B(17,15) = [270,271]$ and $B(17,16) = [288,288]$. For $k = 18$ they are $[266,269]$, $[285,287]$, $[304,305]$ and $[323,323]$, from $q' = 14, 15, 16, 17$. For $k = 19$ they are $[260,265]$, $[280,284]$, $[300,303]$, $[320,322]$, $[340,341]$ and $[360,360]$, from $q' = 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18$. The union of all of these is $$[260,271] \cup [280,288] \cup [300,305] \cup [320,323] \cup [340,341] \cup \{360\},$$ which is disjoint from every remaining candidate. So each remaining candidate attains all of $1, \dots, 19$ and misses $20$, which means $g(N) = 20$. The number of such $N$ is $4 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 32$. The answer is $32$. Why this works. floor-function, casework: a missed value is exactly an interval of $N$ on which two neighbouring floors agree, so the problem becomes comparing explicit blocks case by case.
